heading: 1.1.1.2. Call history

List calls which have finished. There are a wide range of options to filter and sort results, to help you find
the information you need.

results and system load.

include taxes.

text:
1.1.1.3. Control Panel
View and control calls in real-time with drag-and-drop to redirect calls, hang up calls, or initiate new
calls.
These sections are always displayed, even when they are empty:
• Active calls. Each call shows these details:
◦ Participating parties.
◦ Start time.
◦ Duration.
◦ Call direction, which can be inbound, outbound, or internal.
• Telephone lines. Only the phones having the “Show in control panel” setting enabled will be listed.
For each phone, we can see these:
◦ Different colors will be used to indicate if the phone is either unregistered, registered, or
actively participating in a call.
◦ If the phone is active, it will present the main details of the corresponding call.
• Any number. You can enter any arbitrary number, to be dialled if a call or telephone is dragged
onto this section.
Sections for these features will appear only when they have at least one instance with the “Show in

• SIP addresses.
• Feature codes.
• Conferences.
• Hunt groups.
• IVR menus.
• Mailboxes.
• Numbers.
• Page groups.
• Pattern menus.
• Plugins.
• Queues.
• Unlimited access.

• Drag a call onto a telephone line to redirect it.

1.1.1.4. Make a call
You can request a call be made using the web interface.
• Go to Calls and messages » Calls » Make a call.
• Choose the first destination to call. These two options are offered:
◦ Telephone. In this case, select the telephone line to use from the “Telephone line” field.
◦ Number. In this case, enter the phone number in the “Number” field. This can be an arbitrary
number, which will be routed as though you had dialed it from a telephone.
• For the “When answered, forward to” field, enter a number to transfer to once the first destination
has answered. This can be an arbitrary number, such as an external number, or one of the
• features offered by the system, like a number, a feature code, or a telephone line.
• Select the callerid number to display on the first call. Choose Withheld if you do not want the
number displayed.
• If the first destination is a number, select the callerid number to display on the second call. Choose
Withheld if you do not want the number displayed.
• If the first destination is a telephone, choose whether it will be requested to auto-answer.
• Click the “Make a call” button. The first destination should ring within a few seconds. After it
answers, the second destination should ring.

1.1.2.1. Send Email
Send emails directly from the web interface. The system will send the emails asynchronously once the
request is submitted.
You should be aware of the recommended practices in the industry for sending bulk emails, so that you
can deliver useful information to your target audience without causing spam issues.
To send an email
• Go to Calls and messages » Send » Send emails.
• Choose the destination. See below more details.
• Fill in the email attributes (from address, subject, and body).
• Check the field for the disclaimer text to confirm that you have previously tested this email with a
destination address of your own, before attempting to send it to multiple destinations.
• Click the “Send” button.
Destination types
• Myself.
• All users in my customer.
• All users, recursive.
• Billing contacts of our customers.
• Billing contacts of our customers, recursive.
• Technical contacts of our customers.
• Technical contacts of our customers, recursive.
• A file of email addresses. You will be able to upload a text file containing one email address per
line.
• A list of email addresses. You will be able to directly enter email addresses, one per line.
The actual email addresses of contacts and users will be taken from the stored details for customer and
user profiles. Those details can be updated as needed in their corresponding editing pages.

Feature codes are short numbers that are easy for users to remember and can be used for a wide
variety of purposes. For example, you can set “123” to forward to a hunt group of all telephone lines. By

create a feature code with the same number for a different purpose.

1.2.1.4. Speed dials
Speed dials allow users to dial destinations using fewer key presses. They also allow inbound calls from
that destination to have their caller name forced to a particular value, creating a “nickname” for calls from
that destination that is shown on handsets.
Speed dials can be shared, affecting all users within this customer, or they can be specific to one
telephone line. This page discusses shared speed dials. Speed dials specific to one telephone line can
be edited using the link at the bottom of the edit telephone line page.
The “Provision models” setting on the configuration page allows you to enable automatic telephone
provisioning, which can include speed dials in the data passed to the telephone being provisioned.
To add a new speed dial
• Go to Devices and numbers » Numbers » Speed dials.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ The speed dial number that users will dial. This is typically one or two digits.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ What type of button on the handset to use for this speed dial.
◦ The destination to call.
◦ Optionally, a caller name to force for calls from this destination.
• Click the “Save” button.

1.2.2.1. Provisioning
Provisioning templates allow you to configure the data sent to telephone handsets when they request
provisioning.
Best practice is to avoid editing the default templates, and instead add new templates with the template
data copied from one of the defaults.
To add a new provisioning template
• Go to Devices and numbers » Devices and accounts » Provisioning.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
• A name for template.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether it may be used by your customer only or by all customers.
◦ Which model of handsets may use this template.
◦ The priority of the template. If a telephone line is set to “Automatic”, the highest priority
template for the appropriate model will be used.
◦ The template data to send. Any templates which will be served via HTTP must start with a
“Content-type” header, followed by a blank line.
◦ What position telephone lines start at. This is typically 1, but may be 0 for some handsets. If
“MAC address suffix is absolute” is chosen, then a telephone line with MAC address
“00:11:22:33:44:55-6” will be provisioned at position 6.
◦ What position speed dials start at. This is typically 1.
◦ How many speed dials to allow.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Set any telephone lines to use this provisioning template, or leave them at “Automatic”.

heading: 1.2.2.2. Remote access
text:
1.2.2.2. Remote access
Remote access allows you to call into the system and then make calls out. This takes one of three forms:
• A number that you call, and a menu then asks you for a destination number to call. This is the
most common use for remote access; if in doubt use this type.
• The system calls you back. You dial the remote access number from an approved number, and
hang up once you hear it ring. The system will then call you back. Once you answer you can enter
the destination number to call.
• The system directly calls the destination number after stripping off the authentication prefix. This
type is only used to accept outbound calls from customers’ SIP devices that cannot use normal
SIP authentication. In this case, the device can prefix a secret authentication code to the
destination number.
To add a new remote access account
• Go to Devices and numbers » Devices and accounts » Remote access.
• Click the “New” button.

heading: 1.2.2.3. SIP addresses

1.2.2.3. SIP addresses
SIP addresses allow external callers to call in using SIP URIs of the form @. This feature must be
enabled by the system administrator before being used, via the “Enable external SIP sources” setting on
the configuration page.
To add a new SIP address
• Go to Devices and numbers » Devices and accounts » SIP addresses.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ The SIP URI to be called. The user part is free-form letters, numbers, underscores, dashes,
and dots, and must begin with a letter. The domain part must be one of the domains that the
system administrator has enabled for SIP addresses.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ The owner. This user may edit the SIP address even if they are not an administrator.
◦ Whether to screen calls. If set to yes, the user answering will be asked if they wish to accept
the call.
◦ Optionally force the caller’s callerid. This should normally be set to “Original”.
◦ Optionally set the caller’s name. This allows users on a SIP telephone to see which number
the call came from. If not set, the caller name supplied by the caller will be used.
◦ Whether the caller name setting above replaces the caller name supplied by the caller,
prepends to it, or appends to it.
◦ Optionally hang up the call after a certain number of minutes.
◦ Which record group to use to record calls, if you have any.
◦ Which music to play to callers on hold, if you have any.
◦ Whether to display this address on the control panel.
◦ The destination to route calls to this SIP address to.
• Click the “Save” button.

1.3.1.1. Call Recording
Calls can be recorded in real time, and then emailed or downloaded as .wav files. Before enabling call
recording you should check legal requirements in your area regarding use and prior warning to call
participants.
To configure call recording
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Call recording.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the record group.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Optionally an owner for the group, who will be allowed to access its recordings.
◦ Which calls to record.
◦ The percentage of calls to record. This is useful if you only want to record a fraction of calls,
for training purposes. The “on demand only” option means no calls will be recorded unless
requested during the call.
◦ The default expiry time. After a recording expires, it is deleted automatically. You can
change individual recordings’ expiry times once they have been created.
◦ Optionally, one or more email addresses to email recordings to at the end of each call.
• Click the “Save” button.
• In the settings for your numbers, telephone lines, etc, there will now be a new option for the record
group. Set whichever numbers, telephone lines, etc, you wish to use this group. If a call goes
through more than one number, telephone line, etc, that use different record groups, the call is
recorded to all appropriate groups.

heading: 1.3.1.2. Classes of service
text:
1.3.1.2. Classes of service
Classes of service allow you to control which numbers may be called. The called number is matched
against the prefixes in the class of service, and the longest matching prefix is used. For example, all
calls to international numbers can be forbidden by creating a class of service with your international dial
prefix. Alternatively, a single number can be entered to prevent calls to that number.
To create a class of service
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Classes of service.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the group.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether internal and external calls are allowed by default. At this point you cannot enter
specific prefixes or destinations; see below.
◦ If you have configured any time groups, optionally a time group.

heading: 1.3.1.3. IVR menus
text:
1.3.1.3. IVR menus
IVR menus present a list of options to callers and invite them to choose one by pressing a key. It then
forwards them to the destination you set for that key. Destinations can be other IVR menus, allowing
multiple levels of menu. You can also allow callers to enter a number instead of choosing one of the
available options.
To add a new IVR menu
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » IVR menus.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the menu.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether callers may enter a feature code or telephone line. If this is set to yes, the system
will wait until the time-out even if the caller chooses a menu option. This allows them time to
enter a feature code or telephone line that begins with a digit that could also be a menu
option.
◦ How long to wait for the caller to press a key.
◦ A PIN to allow a permitted caller to change the message played.
◦ Whether to display this IVR menu in the control panel.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Set a number or feature code to route to the IVR menu.
• Return to the list of IVR menus page.
• Click on the IVR menu you have just created.
• Optionally, upload a .wav or .mp3 file that is played to the caller. Alternatively, call the IVR menu
and press the IVR setup key (# by default). You will be asked to enter the PIN above.
• Click on any key you wish to change the destination for.
• Choose the destination for this key.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Repeat for other keys as desired.

heading: 1.3.1.4. Mailboxes
text:
1.3.1.4. Mailboxes
Mailboxes receive voicemail and fax messages. If the owner has an email address set an email with an
attachment is sent for each message received. It’s normal, but not required, to have a mailbox for each
telephone line. More than one telephone line, hunt group, etc, may share a mailbox.
To add a new mailbox
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Mailboxes.
• Click the “New” button.

◦ Optionally a description.

are not an administrator.
◦ Whether to display this mailbox in the control panel.
◦ The settings for the menus to play when calling to retrieve messages.
◦ Where to forward the call if the caller press 0 during the greeting.
◦ If you have any other mailboxes, which mailboxes to receive a duplicate copy of messages
for this mailbox.
◦ How to notify the mailbox owner when a new message arrives.
◦ Optionally a backup (secondary) email address to be notified of new messages.

system will not keep a copy of the voicemail, and only the email sent will have the message.

heading: 1.3.1.5. Music
text:
1.3.1.5. Music
Default music on hold is provided by the system, but you may add your own. You must ensure that you
have permission from the music’s copyright holder before doing this.
To add new music
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Music.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the music that users will see.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether it may be used by your customer only or by all customers.

configuration file.

musiconhold.conf, the class to take from musiconhold.conf.
• Click the “Save” button.
• If the type of the music is normal, you can upload music files for it following these steps:
◦ Click on the name of the new music from the list of available music entries.
◦ Go to the “Music files” section and click the “Upload” link for the first file.
◦ Choose a valid music file and click the “Use or upload” button.
◦ After the file is uploaded, you can play, download, or delete it.

heading: 1.3.1.6. Pattern menus
text:
1.3.1.6. Pattern menus
Pattern menus allow flexible routing based on the called number, calling number, and entered by the
caller. Matching on each can be done on exact strings, substrings, or regular expressions. This allows
call flows built on account numbers, passwords, postal or zip codes, or similar.
To add a new pattern menu
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Pattern menus.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the pattern menu.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ The owner. This user may edit the pattern menu even if they are not an administrator.
◦ Whether to ask the caller to enter digits, and if so how many.
◦ If asking the caller to enter digits, how long a timeout to allow between digits.
◦ Whether to display this pattern menu in the control panel.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Click on the pattern menu you have just created.
• Under the “Patterns” section click the “New” button.

◦ A description for the pattern.

the higher priority pattern is used.

◦ Whether to match the digits and calling/called numbers exactly, by substring, or by regular

• Click the “Save” button.

heading: 1.3.1.7. Pickup groups
text:
1.3.1.7. Pickup groups
If a telephone is ringing or has a call on hold, other telephones in the same pickup group may intercept
the call and bring it to them. Telephones may be in more than one pickup group, and may pick up calls
for any telephones in a group they belong to.
To pick up ringing calls
• Create a new Pickup group.
• Set the group to apply to calls which are ringing.
• Add the telephone lines which should be able to pick up each other’s calls.
• Save the group.
• Dial ** to bring any ringing call to a telephone in the group to this telephone.
• Alternatively, dial *** to bring a ringing call for a specific telephone to this telephone.
To assign holding calls a slot number for picking up:
• Holding calls need to be assigned a slot number that can be dialled to intercept the call. You might
want to choose a consecutive range of numbers such as 6XX for this purpose.
• Create a Feature code.
• Set the code to be the next number in your range for holding calls.
• Set the default destination to be “Holding slot”.
• Save the code.
• Repeat as desired to add more holding slots.
• When a telephone puts a call on hold it will be assigned the first available slot number.
• To view the slot number for a call use the Control panel or subscribe to the slot number using busy
lamps.
To pick up holding calls:
• Create a new Pickup group.
• Set the group to apply to calls which are holding.
• Add the telephone lines which should be able to pick up each other’s calls.
• Save the group.
• Dial the slot number to bring the relevant holding call to this telephone.

1.3.1.8. Sounds
Sound files allow you to keep a collection of useful sounds that can then be used for other purposes

1.3.1.9. Times and dates
Time groups allow numbers and feature codes to be routed to different destinations at different times of
the day or days of the week.
Examples of time groups might be:

• Weekday evenings.

Each time group is made up of one or more time periods, which define when the group is active. The
group is active when any of its time periods are active, and a time period is active when all of its criteria
are met.

heading: 1.3.1.10. Web URLs
text:
1.3.1.10. Web URLs
Have an external web URL dynamically determine how a call should be routed. The system passes
details of the call to the URL, and expects a response with the destination to route the call to. This allows
you to have dynamic routing of calls without the expense and complexity of a separate telephone
system.
To add a new web URL
• Go to Features and tools » Call features » Web URLs.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the web URL.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ A HTTP URL that the system will ask where to route the call.
◦ Optionally, a HTTP URL that the system will inform when the call has been answered.
◦ Optionally, a HTTP URL that the system will inform when the call has been hung up.
◦ How long to wait for the web server before timing out.
◦ A destination to route the call to on timeout or if the web server returns an error.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Set a number or feature code to route to the web URL.
Call flow
• The call will be delivered to the feature, such as a number or feature code, that has “Ask web
URL” set as its destination.
• The system will invoke the routing URL specified using HTTP POST, passing the form fields listed
in the “input fields” section below.
• The web server must respond with a text document with the fields listed in the “output fields”
section below. Normally this document would be dynamically generated using a CGI script or
similar.
• The system will route the call to the destination specified by the text document.
• If the web request takes more than the timeout (5 seconds by default), includi

• dtype: The destination type that sent the call to the URL. For example, “number” or “code”.
• dnumber: The destination number that sent the call to the URL, i.e. the number or feature code.
For some dtypes such as IVR, this will be the ID of the object in the database.
• customer: The ID of the customer.
• machine: The ID of the system machine invoking the URL.
• callid: An identifier for the call. Legs of the same call will have the same callid but may have
different uniqueids.
• uniqueid: An identifier for the call leg within the call. For example, a call in to a queue is a different
call leg to the call out to the queue destination.
• state: The state of the call. URLs invoked at the start of the call will be passed “ring” or “answer”.
URLs at the end of the call with be passed “hangup”.
• patternmenu_digits: If the call passed through a pattern menu that collected DTMF digits from the
caller, the digits collected.
In addition, the following fields will be passed on hang up:
• totaltime: How long the call ran for in seconds, including ringing.
• talktime: How long the call ran for in seconds, excluding ringing. For calls which were not
answered, this will be 0.
• status: The status of the call. Normal values are “answer”, “busy”, “cancel”, “congestion”, or
“noanswer”, though other values indicating routing errors are possible.
• recording: The path to the recording file. If there was no recording, this will be an empty string.
• Other fields may be added in future without warning.

heading: 1.3.2.2. Hunt groups
text:
1.3.2.2. Hunt groups
Hunt groups allow more than one destination to ring at once. Within a hunt group, destinations are
arranged into levels. All destinations within a level are rung at once. The first destination to answer hears
the caller, and the others stop ringing (unlike page groups). If no destinations answer, they stop ringing,
all destinations in the next level are rung, and so on.
To add a new hunt group
• If you wish to record calls to this hunt group, make a record group.
• Go to Features and tools » Multi-way calls » Hunt groups.
• Click the “New” button.

◦ A name for the hunt group.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ The owner. This user may edit the hunt group even if they are not an administrator.
◦ How long each level rings for. This can be overridden per level later.
◦ The hunt group type, which controls the order the levels are rung in. Options are “Linear:
Always start at level 1”, “Circular: Start at next level from previous call”, “Smart linear: Last
level that answered, then linear”, and “Smart circular: Last level that answered, then
circular”.
◦ Which record group to use to record calls, if you have any.
◦ Whether to play ringing or play music to callers while the hunt group rings.
◦ Which music to play to callers on hold, if you have any.

to accept the call. While the caller information is being played, other destinations will
continue to ring. The first destination to accept gets the call, and other destinations are

heading: 1.3.2.4. Queues
text:
1.3.2.4. Queues
Queues allow more callers than available destinations. Callers hear music on hold until a destination is
available to take their call.
To add a new queue
• If you wish to record calls to this queue, make a record group.
• Go to Features and tools » Multi-way calls » Queues.
• Click the “New” button.
• For the “Queue settings” section enter the following:
◦ A name for the queue.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ The owner. This user may edit the queue even without being an administrator.
◦ The priority for the queue. Calls on high priority queues get delivered first. Calls on queues
of the same priority are delivered on a first come, first serve basis.
◦ What order to try queue destinations. The choices are essentially between evenly
distributing calls among all priorities, or always trying the highest priority first and then
working down.
◦ Which destination or destinations to call within each priority. “Ring least recently called first;
all in priority” is the most commonly used. “Ring all destinations at once” will prevent any
calls other than the first one in the queue from ringing a destination.
◦ Whether to request destinations to auto-answer. This only affects local SIP handsets, and
only if the handset supports this feature.
◦ How long to ring each destination for. If a destination does not answer, the call is returned to
the queue and other destinations tried.
◦ Whether to allow destinations to forward calls onwards. This is not recommended as it can
cause loops.
◦ Whether to screen calls. If set to yes, the destination will be asked if they wish to acce

depending on the value previously selected for the “Use same destination for all exit

immediately to either the shared exiting destination or the maximum hold time destination,
depending on the value previously selected for the “Use same destination for all exit
reasons” field.
◦ Whether to exit if no destinations are logged in when the call enters the queue. If you
choose “Yes” and that situation happens, the call will be sent immediately to either the
shared exiting destination or the “No destinations” destination, depending on the value
previously selected for the “Use same destination for all exit reasons” field.
◦ If using the same destination for all exit reasons, the destination to route calls to this queue
to if none of the destinations answer before the maximum hold time, or maximum calls are
reached.
◦ If not using the same destination for all exit reasons, the destination to route calls to this
queue to if the caller presses “*”.

using CIDR netmasks, for example “192.168.0.0/16”. Multiple address and/or ranges can be
entered, separated by spaces and/or commas, for example “10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.1”. Set to “auto”
to automatically use the next IP address that the user logs in from.
• Click the “Save” button.
Deleting users
Select the users you want to delete and apply one of the following:
• Click the “Delete selected” button. If any features have the owner set to this user, they will be
changed to have no owner.
• Click the “Delete selected and their features” button. This way, you will not need to process each
feature owned by the user to either remove that feature or to change its owner to another user.
Choosing this option will permanently delete those features.
Exporting users
By clicking on the “Export as .csv” button you can download a .csv file containing all the users of your
customer. Please note:
• Its first line will be a header line.
• The password column will have empty values for each exported user. This means that the real
user’s passwords can not be known from the export

• No header lines will be accepted. You must remove them before uploading the file.
• The password column will be processed in this way:
• For existing users, the current password stored in the database will be kept if the .csv file has an
empty password value for that user.
• For existing users, the new password value of the .csv file will be used if that value is not empty.
This applies only when overwritting existing users.
• For new users, the .csv file must have valid password values. This also means that in this case
those password values can not be empty.
• All non-empty password values will be validated when creating or updating users, as normally
happens in the system. Rows failing to pass this validation will be rejected.
• All these considerations apply to .csv files exported as described in the previous section. To use a
.csv export as an import you will therefore need to:
• Remove the header line.
• Set a password for new users.
• When the validation process rejects a row, its line number and an error message will be showed to
you.

heading: 1.5.1.2. Calling cards
text:
1.5.1.2. Calling cards
Calling cards allow users to call into the system, be authenticated, and make calls out. They are different
from remote access accounts in that calling cards have their own balance and are billed individually,
whereas remote access uses the general customer balance.
Calling cards belong to groups, which set the properties of the cards, and to batches, which are sets of
cards all generated at the same time. Batches make it easy to send cards for printing.
To add a card group
• If you haven’t already done so, make a rate plan to set how much the cards are charged for calls.
• If you haven’t already done so, set a number to the calling card login. One number is sufficient for
all calling cards on the system, and if you’re a reseller the system owner may already have a
suitable number configured.
• Go to Customer » Commerce » Calling cards.
• Click the “New” button.
• For the “Group settings” section enter the following:
◦ A name for the group.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ The rate plan to use.
◦ Whether the group is locked. If so, cards in the group cannot be used.
◦ The dial plan for outbound calls.
◦ The callerid to use on outbound calls.
◦ The currency the credit limit and charge are in.
◦ The credit limit. This is the amount the card balances are allowed to go below zero.
Normally this should be “0.00”.
◦ Which taxes apply to calls made by cards in this group.
◦ The time factor, which can be used to give customers extra free time. This should normally
be “100”.
◦ A destination to automatically dial. If set, users will not be asked for a destination.

To create a batch or batches of cards
• If you haven’t already done so, make a card group as above.
• Go to Customers » Commerce » Calling cards.
• Click on the “New batch” link of the group you wish the cards to be in. Individual cards can be
moved to different groups later.
• Enter the following:
◦ The number of batches to create.
◦ A name for the batch(es). If you are creating multiple batches, a unique suffix will be added
to each.
◦ Whether to lock the batch(es).
◦ Whether to lock each card made. This is independent of the batch being locked; if any of the
group, batch, or card are locked, the card cannot be used.
◦ The number of cards to make in each batch.
◦ The starting balance for the cards.
◦ The currency the balance is in.
◦ The length of the card numbers. Cards can optionally have PINs to make them more secure.
If you choose not to have PINs, the card numbers should be long enough that they cannot
be guessed.
◦ The method for choosing card numbers. If the cards will not have PINs you must choose
random so that users cannot guess other card numbers if they know one number.
◦ The PIN length in digits. Choose 0 for no PINs.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Click the “Batches” link of the group you added the cards to.
• Click the “Cards” link of the batch you just created.
• From the opened list of cards page, download a .csv file containing the card numbers.
• Send the file to a printer to make the cards.
• Sell the cards via retail outlets.
• Customers can use the cards by calling the number configured above. You may care to have this
number printed on the cards.

heading: 1.5.1.4. Rate plans
text:
1.5.1.4. Rate plans
Rate plans define which features are available to customers and how much these features cost. Each
customer has a rate plan, created and assigned to them by their parent customer.

heading: 1.5.1.5. Requests
text:
1.5.1.5. Requests
Customers can send you requests. When they do, the customer service email address you have set in
their rate plan will be notified. You can then log in to the system web interface, go to the Customers »
Commerce » Requests menu, and view and approve or reject the requests.
Requests to top-up a customer account should be processed using your own payment system. Once
processed you can approve the request and the customer’s balance is automatically increased by the
top-up amount.
1.5.1.6. Search
Search for features in your customer and sub-customers recursively.
Performing a search
• Go to Customers » Commerce » Search.
• Choose the type of feature and its property to search for. There are options for calling cards,
customers, mailboxes, numbers, remote access, telephone lines, unassigned numbers, users, and
vouchers.
• Choose the type of match you want to use on the entered value.
• Fill in the value to search for.
• Click the “Update” button.
When searching users by role, the fields for selecting the type of match and to fill in the value to search
for, will not be displayed. Instead, a field to select one of the existing roles will appear.
The format of the results will vary, depending on the selected type of feature.

When searching for customers, the results page will allow you to change the parent of any of the found
customers by applying these steps:
• Select the customers you want to move.
• Click the “Move selected” button. A new dialog box will be displayed.
• Choose which customer will be the new parent of the selected customers.

1.5.1.7. Support
Allow your customers to contact you using a support ticket system. You’ll be notified by email when they
do, and you both can communicate through the ticket to resolve their query.
To enable support tickets for customers
• From the list of available rate plans, choose the rate plan to configure.
• In the rate plan features, enable “Create support tickets”.
• Save the rate plan features.
To use support tickets
Once the customer has support tickets enabled in their rate plan, they will see a new Help » Support
menu. In this menu, they can create support tickets, update tickets they’ve previously opened, and close
tickets once they’re satisfied that their problem is resolved.
You’ll see a new Customers » Commerce » Support menu, in which you can reply to your customers’
tickets, and close tickets that are resolved. The customer who created the ticket will be notified by email
when you do.
Notes about notifications
• You’ll be notified by email, when customers create or update tickets, to the customer service email

heading: 1.5.1.8. Taxes
text:
1.5.1.8. Taxes
Define taxes which apply to prices charged to your customers. Multiple taxes can be defined, and each
tax can be a percentage, a flat amount, or both.
A tax is only applied to customer transactions if both of the following conditions are met:
• The tax applies to the type of transaction (e.g. a call). This is set on the edit tax page.
• The customer is liable for the tax. This is set on the edit customer page, with the default for newly
created taxes and newly created customers set on the edit tax page.
To create a tax
• Go to Customers » Commerce » Taxes.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the tax.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether resellers can assign this tax to customers.
◦ The rate in percent. This is added to costs to customers.
◦ The amount. This is added to costs to customers after the rate.
◦ The currency the amount is in.
◦ Whether all customers are liable for this tax by default. This can be overridden per customer
later.
◦ Whether all calling cards are liable for this tax by default. This can be overridden per card
group later.
◦ Whether this tax applies to the customer account fees each billing cycle. If you wish to add a
flat amount per customer (for example for the USA’s Universal Service Fund), set this to yes
and all later settings to no.
◦ Whether this tax applies to customer features such as telephones, etc.
◦ Whether this tax applies to call costs.
◦ Whether this tax applies to products. This can be overridden per product later.
◦ Whether this tax applies to charges. This can be overridden per charge later.

heading: 1.5.1.10. Vouchers
text:
1.5.1.10. Vouchers
Vouchers allow you to sell pre-paid services to those who don’t have, or prefer not to use, a credit card.
These are often sold in retail outlets such as supermarkets and convenience stores, and allow
customers to top up their balance on the web interface or via telephone.
To create a batch of vouchers
• Make sure your system has been configured to use customer account numbers. If in doubt, consult
your service provider.
• Go to Customers » Commerce » Vouchers.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the batch.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Whether the batch is locked. If it is, no customers can use the serial numbers of that batch.
After the batch is created you can lock it or unlock it as needed.
◦ The number of vouchers to make.
◦ The length of the voucher serial numbers. These should be long enough that they cannot be
guessed.
◦ The value of each voucher. This is the amount that will be added to the customer’s balance
when used. It should include tax if applicable.
◦ The currency the value is in. If used by a customer using a different currency, the value will
be converted at the time of use.
• Click the “Save” button.

The telephones report lists all telephone lines in your customer and sub-customers recursively, and their

To report on telephone lines

1.6.2.4. Traces
Traces are a powerful tool for debugging telephony problems. They provide a definitive answer to the
question “What happened during this call?”
When taking traces, try to find the simplest scenario that reproduces the problem. For example, if your
problem is unrelated to call recording, turn off call recording during the trace. This will make traces much
easier to follow. In particular, hunt groups and queues can add hundreds of extraneous lines to a trace,
so please avoid using these unless the problem is related to them.

On busy systems, it’s sometimes not possible to take a console trace as there are many other calls. In

• SSH into the Asterisk machine or machines.

useful for logging detailed information to /var/log/asterisk/full.
• Run “tail -f /var/log/asterisk/full” for a few seconds and check that new lines are being added. Hit
Ctrl-C to stop.

possible, avoid having other calls active at the same time as they will confuse th

or port 5070 | tee /tmp/trace.txt”, replacing 1234567 with the account to be traced and /tmp/
trace.txt with the file to write to. On some systems, adding -R may be necessary to prevent
“attempt to drop privileges failed” errors.

For RTP problems, Wireshark can be useful. It works in a similar way to ngrep but can collect many

should be reasonably self-explanatory. It’s useful to run at the system cluster and between a handset
and the NAT device simultaneously. This can show whether the NAT device is blocking inbound SIP or
RTP packets. It can save traces in .pcap format which can be uploaded to support tickets.

heading: 1.7.1.3. Domains
text:
1.7.1.3. Domains
When a new SIP packet arrives, the system needs to decide whether:
• The call is for it, or to be forwarded to an external SIP system. To do this, it looks at the domain of
the SIP request URI. If it matches one of the local domains, it is routed by the system. If not, it is
forwarded to the external system in the request URI.
• The call is from a local user or not. If it is, it should be authenticated, and then allowed to call any
number its class of service allows. If not (for example it is from a DID provider), it should not be
authenticated, but then must not be allowed to make chargeable calls unless forwarded by a
customer’s settings. If the domain of the SIP “From” header is local, it is assumed to be from a
local user.
Therefore you should add a domain for any SIP domain your users’ telephone lines will be using to
connect to the system.
To add a new domain
• Go to Global » Settings » Domains.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ The domain.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ Which customer may use this domain in SIP addresses. If this customer has sub-customers,
they may also use it, recursively.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Update your DNS server to send calls to this domain to the system. If you have a cluster with
multiple machines, use the Kamailio service address. You may use SRV records if you wish.

1.7.1.7. Roles
Roles define what each user on the web interface may see and do. A set of roles such as “System
owner”, “Reseller”, “Administrator”, and “User” are pre-defined, and it is best practice to leave these

To add a new role

text:
1.7.2.3. Outbound groups
An outbound group is a set of external numbers that are billed at the same rate. For example, if calls to
UK land lines are are all billed at the same rate, then “UK land lines” could be an outbound group.
Groups can have multiple time chunks, which allows calls to the group to be billed at different rates at
different times of the day and days of the week.
To add a new outbound group
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ A name for the group.
◦ Optionally a description.
◦ How the group is shown on invoices, for example “National”. If not set, the name is used.
◦ Any tags for the group, separated by spaces, for example “international mobile”. Bulk
changes can subsequently be done by tag.
◦ Whether the group counts towards the free minutes included in each rate plan.
• Click the “Save” button.

the week. If two or more time chunks are active at any time, the one with the highest priority is
used.
Once the group has been created, peers can have prices set for the group, and routes can be set to use
it.
1.7.2.4. Peers
Users often need to make calls to the public telephone network ( PSTN). You may have your own
facilities for this, or you can buy services from one or more carriers. These are companies who will take
your calls and forward them to the PSTN. You can use as many carriers as you wish, for example using
one carrier for most calls, and other carriers who can offer cheaper rates for calls to specific
destinations.

Once the peer has been created, routes can be set to use it.
Independent routing table for peer costs
If possible, the peer’s costs should be configured using the system routing table. This is simpler to
configure, and works with least cost routing ( LCR). However, it may not always be possible to
manipulate the costs table provided by a carrier to match the system routes. If this is the case, then peer

• Change the “Peer has independent costs table” setting to yes.

routing table” link at the bottom of the page.

Note that these costs will not be considered when calculating least cost routing. You may therefore wish
to load approximate pricing according to the system routes as a backup.

heading: 1.7.2.5. Regions
text:
1.7.2.5. Regions
Regions allow you to have Asterisk machines in more than one geographical location, and customers
can then route their calls through the closest set of machines, keeping latency to a minimum and
potentially lowering bandwidth costs. Telephony machines can be in more than one region, and can have
different priorities, allowing failover between machines and regions. All customers are configured and
administered on the central database. Regions are an advanced feature that should only be used after
careful planning.
To configure a new region
• Create any Asterisk machines as needed.
• Go to Global » Routing » Regions.
• Click the “New” button.
• Enter the following:
◦ The name of the region.
◦ Optionally a description.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Click the “Machines” link for the region just created.
• Click on each Asterisk machine in turn, set its priority for this region, then save it. Calls will be
distributed among the highest priority Asterisk machines available to take calls.
Regions do not affect calls made using remote access accounts as the customer is not
necessarily known when the call starts.*

heading: 1.8.1.3. Backups
text:
1.8.1.3. Backups
It is vital that you backup your system frequently so that you can recover the system in the event of
administrator error, catastrophic hardware failure, fire, etc. Disk mirroring on its own is not sufficient as it
does not protect against most failures (it only protects against a single disk failure). The following
backups are recommend:
• Copy /var/lib/enswitch to a remote system daily. If using a cluster with multiple machines, this
should be done from the NFS server. This will copy:
◦ Backups of the database, as Enswitch writes its own database backups to /var/lib/enswitch/
backups.
◦ All other customer data files such as invoices, voicemails and greetings, call recordings, IVR
sound files, etc.
• Backup each machine either weekly or monthly, and also after any major upgrades. This allows
you to recover any machines that are completely lost. At minimum you must back up /etc, but an
entire backup of all local filesystems is recommended.
The actual method used to do the backups is up to the system owner. Using rsync to an off-site machine
is both safe and convenient, but other methods such as tapes or shared disks are also feasible.

text:
1.8.1.6. Callerid only numbers
It can often be useful for users to be able to make external calls from the system using a callerid that is
not a number on the system. For example, a user might want to make a call from a desk handset using
their mobile number as callerid so that any returned calls go to their mobile. This can be done by adding
their mobile number to their customer as a callerid only number.
When configuring this, it’s important to ensure that users cannot use this feature to commit callerid fraud.
To prevent such fraud, only a system administrator may add callerid only numbers. Customers may not
do this for themselves. When adding callerid only numbers, you should always verify that the user does
indeed control the number being added, and add it only to their customer.
To configure a callerid only number
• Go to Global » Routing » Inbound groups.
• Click on the group you wish to add the numbers to.
• Click the “Add numbers” link.
• Choose whether to add a single number, a range of numbers, or a text file containing one number
per line.
• Enter the number, start and end numbers, or the file, and default group, class, and region (if
configured). The group and class must allow customers to set numbers as callerids.
• Set the number purpose to be callerid only.
• Select which customer to add the number or numbers to.
• Click the “Save” button.
• Switch to the customer you added the number or numbers to.
• Set the callerids for any desired features such as telephone lines to the number or numbers
added.

You can configure integration with one or more credit card merchant gateways. Prepaid customers can
then top up their accounts on their own. Postpaid customers who have their payment type set to “Credit

start of each month). If the payment was successful, the invoice is marked as paid. If unsuccessful, it is
marked as payment refused.

PayPal page below. All others need to be enabled as follows:

Configuration. If there is already a setting, add a “,authorizenet” to the end – for example

“Authorize.net”, enter your Authorize.net username and password, and click save.

password.

Account » Payment.

» Customers.
• On the first day of each month, after the monthly invoices have run, use Billing and analysis »
Billing » Invoices report to search for invoices with status “Payment refused”, and contac

card integration should do the same.
Beanstream
• Add “beanstream” to the “Credit card merchant types” setting under Global » Settings »
Configuration. If there is already a setting, add a “,beanstream” to the end – for example
“authorizenet,beanstream”.
• Wait one minute for this setting to take effect.
• Go to Users and account » Account » Commerce, change the merchant account provider to
“Beanstream”, enter your Beanstream username and password, and click save.
• Ask any resellers who have a Beanstream account to do the same, using their username and
password.

When choosing a destination for features such as numbers or feature codes, you may choose any

system. These are:

toggles do not disturb for that telephone or external destination.

does not answer the call.

only affects calls made via queues.

heading: 1.8.1.10. Forwarding to an external
text:
1.8.1.10. Forwarding to an external
extension
Many features allow you to forward to an external number using the “External number” entry box on the
destination selector. You can play DTMF to the destination if this is required to specify a particular
extension. For example, to dial “2125551234” and play DTMF “123” when answered, enter
“2125551234×123” in the external number entry box. Anything after the “x” is taken to be DTMF to play.
You may need to delay the DTMF depending on the menu the far end plays. You can do this by adding a
“w” to the string specified. Each “w” creates a delay of 0.5 seconds. You may specify as many of these
as you wish. For example, “2125551234xwwww1w123” will dial 2125551234, then when answered waits
2 seconds, plays a 1, waits another 0.5 seconds, plays 123, then connects the caller. Some
experimentation may be required to find the correct combination of DTMF and waiting.
1.8.1.11. How billing works
The customer is the basic entity within the system. Each user, telephone line, mailbox, etc, belongs to a
customer. All billing is done per customer, except calling cards, which have their own balance.
Customers are arranged in a tree structure; there is a single system owner, which is usually the
company owning the system installation. This customer then has zero or more customers. These
customers can optionally be resellers with customers of their own, and so on. There is no limit to the
number of levels of resellers.

1.8.1.13. Monitoring events
You can be notified when events take place within the system, such as calls starting, being routed, being
answered, or ending, and text messages being received or sent. More event types are expected to be
added in future. These events are sent to a URL of your choice via HTTP/HTTPS POST. To enable this,
set the URL in the “Send events to URL” setting on the Users and account » Account » Customer page
on the system web interface. One request will be made for each event, passing the fields of the event as
fields in the POST body. Each HTTP/HTTPS request will be made directly from the system machine on
which the event occurs. The response from the URL is ignored, so returning an empty document with
Content-Type text/plain is sufficient.
It’s important that you secure this URL from third parties sending bogus events, either by restricting
access to only the IP addresses of the system machines, or by passing an authentication key as a URL
parameter. It’s also important that the URL replies quickly, as routing of calls is delayed until it responds.

heading: 1.8.1.14. Numbers
text:
1.8.1.14. Numbers
Numbers, also known as DIDs or DDIs, are normal telephone numbers that external callers can use to
call into the system from the PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network). Naturally, these numbers
must be allocated and routed to the system by a carrier. Blocks of numbers in each area code you wish
to offer service should be ordered from providers. These can then be loaded into the system for
customers to choose.
Customers may choose from any spare numbers on the system, and can choose to route the number
they have picked to a telephone line, hunt group, feature, etc. The system owner and resellers may
choose how much customers must pay for numbers in rate plans.
If a user (calling from a SIP telephone, calling card, etc) calls a number that is configured in the system,
the call is normally routed within the system, rather than going to a carrier and back. This is called
“shortcut routing”. The customer or customers (if the called number belongs to a different customer) are
still billed the same amount for the outbound and inbound calls as if the call had gone to the carrier and
back.
To load a new range of numbers
• If you haven’t already done so, make an inbound group and optionally any number classes for the
route.
• Go to Global » Routing » Inbound groups.
• Click on the group you wish to add the numbers to.
• Click the “Add numbers” link.
• Choose whether to add a single number, a range of numbers, or a text file containing one number
per line.
• Enter the number, start and end numbers, or the file, and default group, class, and region (if
configured).

heading: 1.8.1.15. Per-customer parking
text:
1.8.1.15. Per-customer parking
Parking can be done within Enswitch rather than Asterisk, which allows each customer to have their own
range of parking slot numbers. Some customers want this so they can have telephone keys park and
pick up calls from their own parking slot numbers with one press.
Since Enswitch 3.15 parking slots between customers can overlap and do not have to be within one
system-wide range. For example, customer A can use slots 701-799, customer B use slots 700-710, and
customer C use slots 210-250.
Shared parking slots can be created at the system level which are available to all customers. Customer-
specific parking slots are assigned within each customer. When a call is parked the system will try to use
a customer-specific parking slot number, and failing that will use a shared parking slot from the system
level.

“parkpos” range configured in /etc/asterisk/res_parking.conf (Asterisk 13 and later) or /etc/asterisk/
features.conf (Asterisk 11 and earlier) on the Asterisk servers. The actual values used in the range
are not important as they are not the parking slots customers will see. A larger range will allow
more calls to be parked.

heading: 1.8.1.16. Ported numbers
text:
1.8.1.16. Ported numbers
Most systems will not use ported numbers, and this step can be ignored.
You can configure the system to allow customers to add their own numbers which have been ported
from another provider. You can of course always add such numbers for your customers, but this
procedure allows them to do it themselves. Please note that:
• Enswitch has no way of doing the actual porting of the number. This procedure merely allows the
customer to add the number to the system once ported.
• Customers could potentially use this to commit callerid fraud. Only trusted customers should be
allowed to do this.
To configure number porting
• Add a new inbound group, perhaps called “Ported numbers”. Choose which customers will be
allowed to port numbers to this group.
• Either add a new number class, setting “Add ported numbers to this class” to yes, or change an
existing class for this setting. This disables this setting for all other number classes.
• In the rate plan features of any rate plan you wish to allow to use this, set “Port numbers into the
system” to “Allow”.
• Customers will now see a new option “Number ported from another provider” when choosing the
inbound group on signing up or adding a new number. If they choose this, the next page will ask
them to enter the number.
• If a customer adds a ported number, then subsequently deletes it, it is removed from the system
rather than returned to the pool.

text:
1.8.1.20. Speech recognition

options. For example, a caller could say “sales” instead of pressing the DTMF key which corresponds

On your system

• Optionally, set the “Speech recognition maximum distance” global configuration.

and and after following the Features link at the bottom change “Speech recognition” to

• Name HTML is the name using HTML encoding for any accented characters.
• Templates specifies the directory under /etc/enswitch/ where you put your translated templates.
• Config file specifies the filename (without the “.conf”) under /etc/enswitch/languages where you put
your translated en.conf.
• Sounds specifies the directory under /etc/enswitch/sounds where you put your translated sounds.

• Asterisk specifies the language to instruct Asterisk to use.
